# Learning Type 1 Diabetes Through Play

Explore games for ==type 1 diabetes (T1D)== education, self-management and psychosocial learning—and the evidence needed to design better ones. This resource is written for researchers, clinicians, educators and developers.

## Find what you need

1. **[Game catalogue](explorer.html):** compare games by year, language, platform, audience, learning goals, evidence, access and price. Open a row for its gameplay description, developer and sources.
2. **[Evidence map](knowledge/games/evidence-map.qmd):** what studies found about knowledge, coping, behaviour and glycaemic outcomes.
3. **[Learning science](knowledge/design/learning-science.qmd) and [design comparisons](knowledge/comparisons/comparative-analysis.qmd):** how to structure practice, feedback, narrative and progression.
4. **[T1D Physiology and Modelling](knowledge/physiology/index.qmd):** scientific foundations for games that represent glucose or treatment dynamics; not a requirement for every psychosocial game.
5. **[Human factors](knowledge/human-factors/onboarding-and-accessibility.qmd) and [sustainability](knowledge/sustainability/index.qmd):** how to make games easier to enter, use and maintain.

## Evidence and access

Studies and obtainable products often concern different games. The [evidence map](knowledge/games/evidence-map.qmd) separates learning, psychosocial, behavioural and clinical findings; [availability](knowledge/games/availability.qmd) examines the access gap.

## Why this project exists

This knowledge base grew out of research for [T1D Simulator](https://github.com/krauhe/t1d-simulator). Its purpose extends beyond that game: help people discover, develop, evaluate and maintain useful T1D learning experiences, regardless of who creates them.

Our [sustainability hypothesis](knowledge/sustainability/why-games-disappear.qmd) concerns the combined expertise needed to keep games usable after funding or key contributors change. Open evidence, reusable design knowledge and documented evaluation methods are intended to reduce duplicated work.
